newsitem.title: USA: Gore uses wooden image to his advantage.
newsitem.headline: Gore uses wooden image to his advantage.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore has turned his image of being stiff and wooden into a political plus.

When he delivered his address at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago in August, he announced that he would do his version of the popular dance, the Macarena. After standing stiffly at the podium for several seconds, he asked: "Want to see it again?" bringing roars of laughter.
But joking aside, Gore should not be underestimated going into his Wednesday night debate with the more animated Jack Kemp, the Republican vice presidential candidate.

When the administration needed someone to debate billionaire Ross Perot in 1993 on the merits of the North American Free Trade Act (NAFTA), Gore was picked for the job and he quickly got the irritable Texan flustered.
Gore also got experience in a debate of vice presidential candidates in 1992 when he and then-Republican incumbent Dan Quayle played the roles of pit bulls for their bosses.
The 48-year-old Gore's influence on President Bill Clinton cannot be overestimated and already he is being talked about as Clinton's heir apparent for the 2000 election.

On the campaign trail, Gore is an attack dog, using much more inflammatory rhetoric to decry Republicans as extremist. In Chicago, he painted a scene of horrors if Republicans controlled the White House and the Congress they hold now.

"Our personal and religious liberties would be at risk. Medicare would be at risk of withering on the vine. Medicaid would be at risk of being taken away from poor children. Education would be at risk. The environment would be at risk from the polluters that control that coalition," he said.
When he appears with Clinton at campaign rallies, he shows an expertise in lathering up the crowd for Clinton far removed from his wooden image.

He likes to tell a long story about how if Dole were elected it would be a cold day of sleet and toes stubbed on table legs, but if Clinton were to win there would be sunshine, fresh flowers and pleasant music on the radio. Clinton laughs every time he hears it.
He has travelled to his native Tennessee frequently trying to make sure he can deliver his state for Clinton-Gore.

Behind the scenes, White House officials say Gore has been a chief political adviser and has been an advocate for the "sensible center" with the departure of political consultant Dick Morris in a sex scandal six weeks ago.

Gore's chief areas of expertise are the environment, technology and foreign policy. When Russian President Boris Yeltsin was re-elected in June, it was Gore who was the first senior U.S. official to see him.
Clinton often refers to Gore as the best vice president in U.S. history and said he chose the senator from Tennessee as his running mate because he wanted someone "smarter than me."
A recent Rose Garden ceremony offered insight into their close relationship. A reporter asked Clinton a question -- prompting a lengthy response.
Then came a tap on Clinton's shoulder. "Could I say something?" Gore interrupted. He then made some points as Clinton stood by smiling and nodding in agreement.
In the past, no vice president would have dared to do that, certainly not Dan Quayle to President George Bush, nor would Bush have considered doing it as Ronald Reagan's vice president.
In fact, the most remarkable part of the incident was that, in the Clinton White House, it was not considered remarkable at all.
